This PR:

# Add `BLESS` — protect keys from eviction

Adds `BLESS`, a keyspace command family for marking specific keys as
**NO-EVICT** under `maxmemory`. A blessed key is never chosen as an
eviction victim. The protection is stored per-key and survives restart
(RDB/AOF), replication, and slot migration.

| `BLESS CLEAR <key> NO-EVICT` | Turn the flag off | `1` / `0` | WRITE,

# Add `BLESS` — protect keys from eviction

Adds `BLESS`, a keyspace command family for marking specific keys as **NO-EVICT** under `maxmemory`. A blessed key is never chosen as an eviction victim. The protection is stored per-key and survives restart (RDB/AOF), replication, and slot migration.

## Commands

All `since 8.12.0`, container `BLESS`.

| Command | Description | Reply | Flags |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `BLESS SET <key> NO-EVICT` | Turn the flag on | `1` if the key's flag set changed, else `0` | WRITE, DENYOOM, FAST |
| `BLESS CLEAR <key> NO-EVICT` | Turn the flag off | `1` / `0` | WRITE, FAST |
| `BLESS GET <key>` | The key's active flag names (`[]` if none) | array; errors if the key is missing | FAST |
| `BLESS SCAN <cursor> NO-EVICT [COUNT <count>]` | Cursored scan of the current DB's blessed keys carrying the flag | `[cursor, [key ...]]` | — |

- The flag argument is **mandatory** — there is no default.
- `BLESS CLEAR` is intentionally **not** DENYOOM, so you can always unbless to recover under memory pressure.
- `BLESS SCAN` mirrors `SCAN` semantics (`COUNT` is a hint, buckets are emitted whole). Without `COUNT` the whole index is returned in one call with cursor `0`; with `COUNT` it paginates.
- `INFO Stats → blessed_keys` — instance-wide count of blessed keys (replaces the earlier `BLESS COUNT` idea).

withheld_evidence.text:
# Redis Array

For years, Redis has been missing a real indexed data structure for the use cases where the index and the spatial relationship of elements are semantic. Hashes give you random lookups, but you have to store an index as a key, and have no range visibility. Lists give you appending and trimming, but what is in the middle remains hard to access. Streams give you append-only events, which is another (useful, indeed) beast. None of these is what you want when the *position itself* has business meaning — slot 37, step 4, row 18552, day from 2934 to 2949, file line 11, 12, 15 and so forth. And, all those types, for different reasons, are all suboptimal when you want a **ring buffer** able to store the latest N observed samples of something.

Up to now, users found ways (they always do \o/) using the fact that the data structures that are obvious in this universe are also extremely powerful, if well implemented. But this forces compromises. Arrays handle these index-first requirements natively, and usually with much better memory and CPU usage than the workarounds. If the use case is the right one, Arrays often provide much better space, time and usability at the same time.

## Internal encoding

1. When dense, an Array is essentially a more fancy C array. You don't pay anything for storing the index.

withheld_evidence.title: Click events are swallowed by SVG <use> elements in IE
withheld_evidence.text: We've only managed to replicate this in Edge and <=IE11, not Chrome or Firefox. We've created a demo of the issue with [this jsbin](http://jsbin.com/jojosesupe). We're using a common SVG element and linking to it with `xlink:href` as is common with SVG icons. When linking to the icons with a `` tag inside an anchor, all click events on the icon will not bubble to onClick handlers on the anchor. An example: I have a common SVG element with an icon ``. I then make a link containing my icon `'}}>`. As `xlink:href` isn't supported by react yet, we have to use `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. If we now click the SVG **any onClick handlers on the anchor will not run**. A temporary workaround is setting `pointer-events: none` on the SVG element inside the anchor. This might be a dupe of #1509
